newsitem.title: POLAND: NO DEAL YET ON POLAND-EU ROW OVER DAEWOO.
newsitem.headline: NO DEAL YET ON POLAND-EU ROW OVER DAEWOO.

text.p: Warsaw and the EU failed after two days of talks to end a row over duty free imports of car parts for assembly in Poland by South Korean car maker Daewoo, but they said they hoped to settle it by the end of April.

European Union negotiator Sipke Brouwer told reporters after the EU-Poland Association Committee meeting in Warsaw that both sides both hoped to have a solution by April 29, when the Association Council convenes in Brussels.

"We have agreed on a procedure to arrive at a satisfactory solution to be endorsed at the Association Council, with a clear timetable. In the coming one to two weeks, precise steps will have to be taken," Brouwer said.
"If no satisfactory solution is to be found we have some agreements in our European Union that we can invoke," he said.

The European Union objects to a deal by which Poland has allowed South Korea's Daewoo Motor Co to import tens of thousands of car kits a year duty-free, as part of its purchase last year of the FSO car plant in Warsaw.

The EU sees this arrangement, in which entire vehicles made in South Korea are brought whole to Slovenia, dismantled into a few parts for shipping to Poland, imported duty free and then reassembled, as providing unfairly advantageous access for an Asian competitor to the Polish and European market.
Last year, Daewoo assembled about 98,000 cars in Warsaw.

"The question is when is a part to be imported to be considered as a vehicle as such and when is a part considered a spare part. There are international rules and we have transmitted this to Polish side," Brouwer said.
Polish officials said lawyers of both sides would now study international agreements and legal precedents, to try to determine definitions of what constituted a complete car.
Bouwers however praised Poland's progress on settling the issue of the way parts were imported -- a reference to last month's decision by Daewoo to change its rules on imports.
Under new regulations, effective from March 15, car bodies, engines and transmissions would be brought in for assembly in separate transports and not in one as is the case now.
The Daewoo issue is the gravest of several thorny trade disputes which have tarnished Poland's relations with the EU in the last two years as it strove for rapid entry to the bloc.

Brouwer and Poland's representative, Danuta Huebner, said several of these matters had now been cleared up -- including ones concerning Polish recognition of European Union product certificates and an understanding on Poland's fuels sector.

"We clearly feel that trade matters, which have so far dominated, are being replaced...with matters more bound up with cooperation. This is extremely important because it shows we are on a new stage of our cooperation," said Huebner, secretary of the Polish government's European Integration Committee. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
